n: Extracorporeal Membrane Oxygenation in Paediatric Respiratory Failure

faq.a: In low‑resource settings a trained intensivist or paediatrician can perform percutaneous cannulation using ultrasound guidance, but surgical backup is advisable.
faq.q: Can ECMO be started without a cardiothoracic surgeon?

faq.a: No; it is a bridge to recovery while the underlying lung disease is treated.
Switch to a spare circuit immediately; if none are available, consider rapid weaning and maximal conventional ventilation.
faq.q: What if the oxygenator fails during support?

exam: A child with severe malaria‑induced ARDS has PaO₂/FiO₂ = 70 mmHg on FiO₂ 0.95 – what is the next step? — Recognise refractory hypoxaemia; discuss ECMO candidacy and urgent transfer to a centre with ECMO capability.
Explain why VA‑ECMO is preferred over VV‑ECMO in a post‑operative tetralogy of Fallot patient with low cardiac output. — Highlight need for circulatory support in addition to oxygenation.

What laboratory test is essential before starting heparin anticoagulation, and how do you proceed if it is unavailable? — Coagulation profile; use clinical bleeding assessment and low‑dose heparin with ACT monitoring.

A child on ECMO develops unilateral cool leg and absent pulses – what does this indicate and how do you manage it? — Limb ischemia from arterial cannula; consider distal perfusion cannula or repositioning.
During ECMO, the patient’s lactate rises despite normal ABG values – what does this suggest? — Inadequate tissue oxygen delivery; reassess circuit flow and oxygenator function.
Why is high‑dose steroids not routinely used in ECMO for paediatric ARDS? — Lack of mortality benefit and increased infection risk; guidelines recommend supportive care only.
List three common infections in East Africa that may lead to ECMO‑eligible respiratory failure. — Severe pneumonia (Strep pneumoniae), malaria, tuberculosis.
What are the key components of lung‑protective ventilation while a child is on VV‑ECMO? — Low tidal volume 3‑4 mL/kg, FiO₂ ≤ 0.4, PEEP ≈ 10 cmH₂O, permissive hypercapnia.
ai.title: Extracorporeal Membrane Oxygenation in Paediatric Respiratory Failure
ai.subject: Paediatrics
ai.summary: ECMO provides temporary cardiopulmonary support when conventional ventilation fails. In low‑resource settings it is used selectively for severe ARDS, congenital heart disease post‑operative failure, and refractory septic shock in children.

b: VV‑ECMO for isolated respiratory failure
VA‑ECMO for combined cardiac‑respiratory collapse
sections.p: ECMO is a form of extracorporeal life support that oxygenates blood and removes CO₂ while bypassing the lungs (veno‑venous) or both heart and lungs (veno‑arterial). Diagnosis is clinical: child with severe hypoxaemia or hypercapnia despite optimal mechanical ventilation and rescue therapies.

b: OI ≥ 40 or PaO₂/FiO₂ < 80 mmHg despite lung‑protective ventilation → consider ECMO
Refractory hypercapnia (pH < 7.20) despite high‑frequency oscillation or prone positioning
sections.p: Severity is staged by the PaO₂/FiO₂ ratio and the oxygenation index (OI).

b: Severe viral or bacterial pneumonia (including RSV, influenza, pneumococcus)
Malaria‑associated acute lung injury
Tuberculosis meningitis with secondary ARDS
Severe sickle‑cell vaso‑occlusive lung disease
Post‑operative cardiac surgery or congenital heart disease with pulmonary hypertension
sections.p: In East Africa the common precipitants of refractory respiratory failure in children are:

b: Progressive hypoxaemia (SpO₂ < 85 % on FiO₂ ≥ 0.9)
Severe hypercapnia (pCO₂ > 80 mmHg) with acidemia
Increasing work of breathing, tachypnoea, and exhaustion
Hemodynamic instability requiring vaso‑pressors
sections.p: Children deteriorate despite maximal ventilatory support, showing:

t.b: Confirms refractory hypoxaemia/hypercapnia; guides timing of ECMO
Shows diffuse infiltrates or consolidation; helps rule out pneumothorax before cannulation
Assesses cardiac function; determines need for VA‑ECMO
Identifies treatable infections; if unavailable, treat empirically based on local epidemiology
Baseline for anticoagulation; if unavailable, use bedside clotting time and clinical bleeding signs

b: Bleeding from cannulation sites or intracranial haemorrhage
Circuit thrombosis leading to oxygenator failure
Infection of cannulae or bloodstream
Limb ischemia (especially with VA‑ECMO femoral cannula)
Renal failure from low flow or hemolysis
sections.p: Complications increase mortality and must be anticipated.

b: Select VV‑ECMO for isolated lung failure; VA‑ECMO when cardiac output is inadequate
Use heparin infusion targeting ACT 180‑200 s; if heparin unavailable, use low‑dose unfractionated heparin bolus and monitor clinically
Maintain circuit flow 80‑100 mL/kg/min to ensure adequate oxygen delivery
Treat underlying cause: antibiotics for bacterial pneumonia, antimalarials, anti‑TB therapy, exchange transfusion for sickle‑cell crisis
Ventilator strategy during ECMO: low tidal volume (3‑4 mL/kg), FiO₂ ≤ 0.4, PEEP 10 cmH₂O to allow lung rest
sections.p: ECMO is a bridge to recovery; management follows three pillars: cannulation, anticoagulation, and supportive care.

b: Gradual weaning of ventilator settings over 24‑48 h
Daily neuro‑vascular checks for limb ischemia resolution
Vaccination and prophylaxis (e.g., pneumococcal, influenza) to reduce future severe infections
Education of caregivers on early signs of respiratory distress
sections.p: After decannulation, monitor for rebound respiratory failure and organ dysfunction.

b: Continuous Renal Replacement Therapy (CRRT) – renal support only, no gas exchange
High‑frequency oscillatory ventilation – invasive lung ventilation, not extracorporeal
sections.p: ECMO is sometimes mixed up with other extracorporeal supports.

b: Normal SpO₂ on high FiO₂ may mask poor tissue oxygen delivery; always check lactate
Transient improvement after prone positioning can delay ECMO decision
Coagulation tests may be normal despite circuit‑induced micro‑thrombi; watch for visual clotting in the oxygenator
sections.p: Certain bedside findings may give false reassurance.

ai.clinicalScope: Extracorporeal Membrane Oxygenation (ECMO) for children with refractory severe respiratory failure in low‑resource East African hospitals
whenToSeekHelp: Uncontrolled bleeding or sudden loss of circuit flow
